title: Git Objects: Blobs, Trees, and Commits
description: Understand the three core Git object types and how Git's content-addressable database stores your repository.

data.text: Git is often treated as a black box, but its internal design is elegant and surprisingly simple. Every piece of data in a Git repository is stored as an object inside the .git/objects directory. Git uses SHA-1 (or SHA-256) hashes as object IDs, so the contents themselves determine the address.

data.title: Why This Matters
data.text: Understanding the object model helps you diagnose repository corruption, recover data after force pushes, and write scripts that interact directly with Git's storage layer.
Every object in Git is one of four types. Each is identified by its type and SHA-1 hash, making the store content-addressable and inherently verifiable.

data.title: Object types at a glance
items: **blob** — Raw file content. A blob has no filename; it is purely the bytes of a file.
**tree** — A directory listing. Maps filenames to blobs (or other trees) and stores Unix mode bits.
**commit** — A snapshot with author, committer, message, parent commits, and a pointer to a top-level tree.
**tag** — A signed or unsigned reference to another object, usually a commit, used for releases.

data.title: Inspect objects with git cat-file
data.code:
# Show the type and size of the latest commit
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -s HEAD

# Pretty-print a commit
git cat-file -p HEAD

# Show the tree referenced by a commit
git ls-tree HEAD

# Find the blob for a specific file
git ls-tree HEAD src/Program.cs

data.text: A commit does not store a diff. It stores a pointer to a tree plus parent commit IDs. Git reconstructs changes by comparing the trees of successive commits. This means every commit contains the full logical state of the project at that moment.

data.title: Why snapshots, not diffs?
data.text: Snapshot-based storage makes operations like checkout, diff, and log fast and reliable. Git never needs to reconstruct a file's contents by patching a series of diffs — it reads the tree directly.

New objects are stored as loose files in .git/objects/AB/CDEF... where AB is the first two characters of the SHA-1 and CDEF... is the remainder. Once enough loose objects accumulate, Git consolidates them into pack files for efficiency.

data.title: Count objects and check repository integrity
data.code:
# Count objects in the object database
git count-objects -v

# Verify every object is readable and checksums match
git fsck --full

# Count loose vs packed objects
git count-objects

terms.definition: A storage scheme where the address of an object is derived from its contents. If contents change, the address changes.
Low-level Git commands (cat-file, hash-object, update-ref) that operate directly on objects. Use with care.
A single-file Git object stored uncompressed in .git/objects/. Contrasts with pack files.

items.question: Does Git store diffs or full file snapshots?
items.answer: Git stores full snapshots via tree objects. Diffs are calculated on demand by comparing trees. This is a fundamental design decision that makes Git fast and reliable.

items.question: What hash algorithm does Git use?
items.answer: Git traditionally uses SHA-1. As of Git 2.29+ there is experimental SHA-256 support, but SHA-1 remains the default on most systems.

items.question: Can two blobs have the same hash?
items.answer: In theory SHA-1 collisions are possible, but in practice Git's object model makes collisions extremely unlikely. Git also stores the object type alongside the hash, reducing collision risk further.

items.question: Is there a limit to how many objects a repository can have?
items.answer: No hard limit, but very large numbers of loose objects slow down Git. Git automatically runs pack compression via git gc to keep things efficient.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Git stores everything as blobs, trees, commits, and tags in a content-addressable store.
A commit is a pointer to a tree plus parent IDs — not a diff.
Objects are addressed by their SHA-1 hash, making the store self-verifying.
Loose objects accumulate over time; git gc consolidates them into pack files.
